raphus:eswiki:9.title: Raphus cucullatus (El dodo y la cultura)

facts.statement: The dodo became extinct in 1662.
facts.quote: extinct: 1662

facts.statement: The scientific species name of the dodo is cucullatus.
facts.quote: species: cucullatus

facts.statement: The dodo was first described by Carl Linnaeus in 1758.
facts.quote: authority: (Linnaeus, 1758)

facts.statement: The dodo was an extinct flightless bird found only on the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean.
facts.quote: The dodo (Raphus cucullatus) is an extinct flightless bird that was endemic to Mauritius, an island east of Madagascar in the Indian Ocean.

facts.statement: The dodo's closest relative was the extinct and flightless Rodrigues solitaire.
facts.quote: The dodo's closest relative was the also-extinct and flightless Rodrigues solitaire.

facts.statement: The dodo and the Rodrigues solitaire formed the subtribe Raphina within the pigeon and dove family Columbidae.
facts.quote: The two formed the subtribe Raphina, a clade of extinct flightless birds that are a part of the group that includes pigeons and doves (the family Columbidae).

facts.statement: The first recorded sighting of the dodo occurred in 1598 when Dutch sailors encountered it.
facts.quote: The first recorded mention of the dodo was by Dutch sailors in 1598.

facts.statement: Subfossil evidence indicates the dodo stood between 62.6 and 75 cm tall and weighed between 10.6 and 17.5 kg.
facts.quote: Subfossil remains show the dodo measured about 62.6 - 75 cm in height and may have weighed 10.6 - 17.5 kg in the wild.

facts.statement: The dodo used gizzard stones to digest a diet of fruits and lived in the woods of drier coastal areas of Mauritius.
facts.quote: It used gizzard stones to help digest its food, which is thought to have included fruits, and its main habitat is believed to have been the woods in the drier coastal areas of Mauritius.

facts.statement: One historical account suggests the dodo laid a single egg per clutch.
facts.quote: One account states its clutch consisted of a single egg.

facts.statement: Researchers presume the dodo lost the ability to fly due to abundant food and a lack of predators on Mauritius.
facts.quote: It is presumed that the dodo became flightless because of the ready availability of abundant food sources and a relative absence of predators on Mauritius.

facts.statement: A dried head is the only remaining soft tissue specimen of the dodo.
facts.quote: Among these is a dried head, the only soft tissue of the dodo that remains today.

facts.statement: Most subfossil dodo remains have been collected from the Mare aux Songes swamp on Mauritius.
facts.quote: Since then, a large amount of subfossil material has been collected on Mauritius, mostly from the Mare aux Songes swamp.

facts.statement: In 1842, Johannes Theodor Reinhardt proposed the dodo was a ground pigeon based on a skull found in the Natural History Museum of Denmark.
facts.quote: In 1842, Danish zoologist Johannes Theodor Reinhardt proposed that dodos were ground pigeons, based on studies of a dodo skull he had discovered in the collection of the Natural History Museum of Denmark.

facts.statement: Strickland and Melville established that the dodo shared many anatomical features with pigeons.
facts.quote: Strickland and Melville established that the dodo was anatomically similar to pigeons in many features.

facts.statement: The dodo differed from other pigeons primarily by having small wings and a large beak relative to its skull.
facts.quote: The dodo differed from other pigeons mainly in the small size of the wings and the large size of the beak in proportion to the rest of the cranium.

facts.statement: In 2024, the subtribe Raphina was established to contain only the dodo and the Rodrigues solitaire.
facts.quote: In 2024, the new subtribe Raphina was created to include only the dodo and the solitaire.

facts.statement: The exact appearance and behavior of the dodo remain unresolved because historical portraits vary and few were drawn from live specimens.
facts.quote: Since these portraits vary considerably, and since only some of the illustrations are known to have been drawn from live specimens, the dodos' exact appearance in life remains unresolved, and little is known about its behaviour.

facts.statement: During the 19th century, the Rodrigues solitaire and Réunion solitaire were sometimes classified as the same species as the dodo under different genus names.
facts.quote: Throughout the 19th century, several species were classified as congeneric with the dodo, including the Rodrigues solitaire and the Réunion solitaire, as Didus solitarius and Raphus solitarius, respectively (Didus and Raphus being names for the dodo genus used by different authors of the time).

facts.statement: Genetic analysis placed the dodo within the pigeon family (Columbidae) alongside the Rodrigues solitaire.
facts.quote: Comparison of mitochondrial cytochrome b and 12S rRNA sequences isolated from a tarsal of the Oxford specimen and a femur of a Rodrigues solitaire confirmed their close relationship and their placement within the Columbidae.

facts.statement: The absence of competing mammalian herbivores on the Mascarene Islands allowed the dodo to evolve large size and flightlessness.
facts.quote: The lack of mammalian herbivores competing for resources on these islands allowed the solitaire and the dodo to attain very large sizes and flightlessness.

facts.statement: Most historical representations depict the dodo with greyish or brownish plumage and a tuft of curly light feathers on its rear.
facts.quote: According to most representations, the dodo had greyish or brownish plumage, with lighter primary feathers and a tuft of curly light feathers high on its rear end.

facts.statement: The dodo had a naked grey head, a beak colored green, black, and yellow, and stout yellowish legs with black claws.
facts.quote: The head was grey and naked, the beak green, black and yellow, and the legs were stout and yellowish, with black claws.

facts.statement: Subfossil remains indicate that dodos stood between 62.6 and 75 cm tall.
facts.quote: Subfossil remains and remnants of the birds that were brought to Europe in the 17th century show that dodos were very large birds, measuring about 62.6 - 75 cm in height.

facts.statement: A 1993 study by Bradley C. Livezey estimated male dodos weighed 21 kg and females 17 kg.
facts.quote: In 1993, Bradley C. Livezey proposed that males would have weighed 21 kg and females 17 kg.

facts.statement: There is ongoing scientific controversy regarding the accurate weight estimates of wild dodos.
facts.quote: This has also been questioned, and there is still controversy over weight estimates.

facts.statement: The Dutch name "Walghvoghel" was first recorded in 1598 by Vice admiral Wybrand van Warwijck in his journal.
facts.quote: One of the original names for the dodo was the Dutch "Walghvoghel", first used in the journal of Dutch Vice admiral Wybrand van Warwijck, who visited Mauritius during the Second Dutch Expedition to Indonesia in 1598.

facts.statement: Mathurin Jacques Brisson established the genus name Raphus in 1760, leading to the current scientific name Raphus cucullatus.
facts.quote: Mathurin Jacques Brisson coined the genus name Raphus (referring to the bustards) in 1760, resulting in the current name Raphus cucullatus.

facts.statement: Sir Thomas Herbert claimed in his 1634 travelogue that the Portuguese had called the bird "dodo" during their 1507 visit to Mauritius.
facts.quote: The English writer Sir Thomas Herbert was the first to use the word dodo in print in his 1634 travelogue claiming it was referred to as such by the Portuguese, who had visited Mauritius in 1507.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest the name "dodo" is an onomatopoeia of the bird's two-note call resembling "doo-doo".
facts.quote: It has also been suggested that dodo was an onomatopoeic approximation of the bird's call, a two-note pigeon-like sound resembling "doo-doo".

facts.statement: Feathers from the Oxford specimen head were found to be pennaceous (stiff) rather than downy, similar to other pigeons.
facts.quote: A study of the few remaining feathers on the Oxford specimen head showed that they were pennaceous rather than plumaceous (downy) and most similar to those of other pigeons.

facts.statement: The dodo had a robust skull with a hooked bill and a short cranium relative to its jaws.
facts.quote: The skull of the dodo differed much from those of other pigeons, especially in being more robust, the bill having a hooked tip, and in having a short cranium compared to the jaws.

facts.statement: The dodo's nostril openings were elongated along the beak and lacked a bony septum.
facts.quote: The openings of the bony nostrils were elongated along the length of the beak, and they contained no bony septum.

facts.statement: The dodo's scleral rings were formed by eleven small bones, a number similar to other pigeons.
facts.quote: The scleral rings inside the eye were formed by eleven ossicles (small bones), similar to the amount in other pigeons.

facts.statement: The dodo's neck had well-developed muscle and ligament attachment areas, likely to support its heavy skull and beak.
facts.quote: The neck had well-developed areas for muscle and ligament attachment, probably to support the heavy skull and beak.

facts.statement: The dodo's sternum was large in absolute size but small relative to its body compared to flying pigeons.
facts.quote: The sternum was large, but small in relation to the body compared to those of much smaller pigeons that are able to fly.

facts.statement: The dodo's pelvis was wider than that of the Rodrigues solitaire but proportionally similar to some smaller flying pigeons.
facts.quote: The pelvis was wider than that of the solitaire and other relatives, yet was comparable to the proportions in some smaller, flighted pigeons.

facts.statement: The dodo had proportionally shorter neck and legs and lacked the knob found on the solitaire's wrists.
facts.quote: The dodo's neck and legs were proportionally shorter, and it did not possess an equivalent to the knob present on the solitaire's wrists.

facts.statement: The traditional image of the dodo as a very fat and clumsy bird may be exaggerated.
facts.quote: The traditional image of the dodo is of a very fat and clumsy bird, but this view may be exaggerated.

facts.statement: Some depictions of dodos may show them with puffed feathers used for display behavior.
facts.quote: It has also been suggested that the images might show dodos with puffed feathers, as part of display behaviour.

facts.statement: Studies of the dodo's leg bone strength suggest it could run quite fast.
facts.quote: Studies of the cantilever strength of its leg bones indicate that it could run quite fast.

facts.statement: Although some dodo bones show healed fractures, the species had weak pectoral muscles and reduced wings compared to the solitaire.
facts.quote: Though some dodo bones have been found with healed fractures, it had weak pectoral muscles and more reduced wings in comparison.

facts.statement: The dodo likely used its large, hooked beak for territorial disputes rather than wing combat.
facts.quote: The dodo may instead have used its large, hooked beak in territorial disputes.

facts.statement: Most contemporary descriptions of the dodo come from ship logs and journals of Dutch East India Company vessels docked in Mauritius during Dutch rule.
facts.quote: Most contemporary descriptions of the dodo are found in ship's logs and journals of the Dutch East India Company vessels that docked in Mauritius when the Dutch Empire ruled the island.

facts.statement: One of the earliest accounts of the dodo comes from van Warwijck's 1598 journal.
facts.quote: One of the earliest accounts, from van Warwijck's 1598 journal, describes the bird as follows:

facts.statement: The Dutch painter Roelant Savery was the most prolific and influential dodo illustrator, creating at least twelve depictions.
facts.quote: The Dutch painter Roelant Savery was the most prolific and influential illustrator of the dodo, having made at least twelve depictions, often showing it in the lower corners.

facts.statement: A famous 1626 painting by Roelant Savery, known as Edwards's Dodo, has become the standard image of the dodo.
facts.quote: A famous painting of his from 1626, now called Edwards's Dodo as it was once owned by the ornithologist George Edwards, has since become the standard image of a dodo.

facts.statement: An Indian Mughal painting rediscovered in the Hermitage Museum in 1955 depicts a dodo alongside native Indian birds.
facts.quote: An Indian Mughal painting rediscovered in the Hermitage Museum, St. Petersburg, in 1955 shows a dodo along with native Indian birds.

facts.statement: Historical differences in dodo depictions led to theories about sexual dimorphism, age traits, seasonal variation, and different species, but these are not accepted today.
facts.quote: Differences in the depictions led ornithologists such as Anthonie Cornelis Oudemans and Masauji Hachisuka to speculate about sexual dimorphism, ontogenic traits, seasonal variation, and even the existence of different species, but these theories are not accepted today.

facts.statement: Variations in historical accounts make it impossible to determine if details like beak markings or tail feather forms reflect reality, age, or sex.
facts.quote: Because details such as markings of the beak, the form of the tail feathers, and colouration vary from account to account, it is impossible to determine the exact morphology of these features, whether they signal age or sex, or if they even reflect reality.

facts.statement: Julian Hume argued that the living dodo had slit nostrils, citing specific historical images as evidence.
facts.quote: Hume argued that the nostrils of the living dodo would have been slits, as seen in the Gelderland, Cornelis Saftleven, Savery's Crocker Art Gallery, and Mansur images.

facts.statement: Based on weight estimates, it is suggested the male dodo could live to 21 and the female to 17 years.
facts.quote: Based on weight estimates, it has been suggested the male could reach the age of 21, and the female 17.

facts.statement: The dodo likely ate fallen fruits, nuts, seeds, bulbs, and roots.
facts.quote: In addition to fallen fruits, the dodo probably subsisted on nuts, seeds, bulbs, and roots.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the dodo may have also eaten crabs and shellfish.
facts.quote: It has also been suggested that the dodo might have eaten crabs and shellfish, like their relatives the crowned pigeons.

facts.statement: Contemporary sources state the dodo used gastroliths to aid digestion.
facts.quote: Several contemporary sources state that the dodo used gastroliths (gizzard stones) to aid digestion.

facts.statement: A 2016 study found the dodo's upper jaw was rhynchokinetic, affecting its feeding behavior.
facts.quote: In 2016, the palaeontologist Leon Claessens and colleagues found that skeletal elements of the dodo's upper jaw appear to have been rhynchokinetic (movable in relation to each other), which must have affected its feeding behaviour.

facts.statement: The dodo's beak could withstand high force loads, indicating a diet of hard food.
facts.quote: The beak also appears to have been able to withstand high force loads, which indicates a diet of hard food.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the dodo's visual abilities reflect a shift to crepuscular activity to avoid heat and competition.
facts.quote: The visual abilities of the dodo possibly reflect a shift towards becoming more crepuscular (active during dusk and dawn), which could help it avoid intense heat during the day and forage when there was less competition from other species.

facts.statement: The dodo and solitaire likely had better low-frequency hearing due to their large size.
facts.quote: The dodo and solitaire shared better hearing in low frequencies, possibly because their larger size resulted in low-frequency vocalisation (confirmed for the latter by historical accounts).

facts.statement: The dodo probably nested on the ground because it was flightless and had no mammalian predators on Mauritius.
facts.quote: As it was flightless and terrestrial and there were no mammalian predators or other kinds of natural enemy on Mauritius, the dodo probably nested on the ground.

facts.statement: The dodo is proposed to be K-selected, producing few offspring that required parental care until maturity.
facts.quote: Because of the possible single-egg clutch and the bird's large size, it has been proposed that the dodo was K-selected, meaning that it produced few altricial offspring, which required parental care until they matured.

facts.statement: A 2017 study used bone histology and other data to recover information about the dodo's life history.
facts.quote: A 2017 study examined the histology of thin-sectioned dodo bones, modern Mauritian birds, local ecology, and contemporary accounts, to recover information about the life history of the dodo.

facts.statement: Dodo chicks grew rapidly to near-adult size and reached sexual maturity before the Austral summer or cyclone season.
facts.quote: The chicks grew rapidly, reaching robust, almost adult, sizes, and sexual maturity before Austral summer or the cyclone season.

facts.statement: Adult dodos that had just bred moulted around March.
facts.quote: Adult dodos which had just bred moulted after Austral summer, around March.

facts.statement: Stanley Temple hypothesized the tambalacoque tree depended on the dodo for seed germination.
facts.quote: Stanley Temple hypothesised that it depended on the dodo for its propagation, and that its seeds would germinate only after passing through the bird's digestive tract.

facts.statement: Reports from the 1940s found tambalacoque seeds could germinate without passing through a digestive tract.
facts.quote: Temple overlooked reports from the 1940s that found that tambalacoque seeds germinated, albeit very rarely, without being abraded during digestion.

facts.statement: Other researchers contested Temple's hypothesis, suggesting the tree's decline was exaggerated or seeds were distributed by other extinct animals.
facts.quote: Others have contested his hypothesis and suggested that the decline of the tree was exaggerated or seeds were also distributed by other extinct animals such as Cylindraspis tortoises, fruit bats, or the broad-billed parrot.

facts.statement: Strahm and Cheke stated in 1991 that the tambalacoque tree had germinated hundreds of times since the dodo's extinction, discrediting Temple's view.
facts.quote: The ecologists Wendy Strahm and Anthony Cheke stated in 1991 that while rare, the tree has germinated since the demise of the dodo and numbers several hundred, not 13 as claimed by Temple, hence, discrediting Temple's view as to the dodo and the tree's sole survival relationship.

facts.statement: A 2023 study noted the dodo's loss negatively impacted native seed dispersal because introduced species handle seeds differently.
facts.quote: In 2023, the biologist Julia H. Heinen and colleagues noted that the loss of the dodo (which probably preferred large seeds and fruits) and other native frugivores had a negative impact on seed dispersal of native plants due to the lack of species with their gape size, and that seed-handling of introduced species was ecologically different, and therefore does not restore this functionality there.

facts.statement: The dodo likely lived in the woods of the drier coastal areas on the south and west coasts of Mauritius.
facts.quote: The preferred habitat of the dodo is unknown, but old descriptions suggest that it inhabited the woods on the drier coastal areas of south and west Mauritius.

facts.statement: Subfossil bones found in highland caves indicate that the dodo once lived on mountains.
facts.quote: Subfossil bones have also been found inside caves in highland areas, indicating that it once occurred on mountains.

facts.statement: Excavations suggest dodos became trapped in the Mare aux Songes swamp while trying to reach water during a severe drought approximately 4,200 years ago.
facts.quote: Subsequent excavations suggested that dodos and other animals became mired in the Mare aux Songes while trying to reach water during a long period of severe drought about 4,200 years ago.

facts.statement: Reports published in 1601 contain the first published illustration of the dodo.
facts.quote: They appear in reports published in 1601, which also contain the first published illustration of the bird.

facts.statement: Although dodos were easy to catch, their powerful beaks posed a danger to hunters.
facts.quote: Dodos were easy to catch, but hunters had to be careful not to be bitten by their powerful beaks.

facts.statement: Documents published in 2014 confirmed that a dodo sent to Nagasaki, Japan, in 1647 arrived alive.
facts.quote: One dodo was reportedly sent as far as Nagasaki, Japan, in 1647, but it was long unknown whether it arrived. Contemporary documents first published in 2014 proved the story, and showed that it had arrived alive.

facts.statement: The dodo was entirely fearless of humans because it evolved in isolation from significant predators.
facts.quote: Like many animals that evolved in isolation from significant predators, the dodo was entirely fearless of humans.

facts.statement: Archaeological investigations have found scant evidence that humans were the main cause of the dodo's extinction, despite reports of mass killings for provisions.
facts.quote: Although some scattered reports describe mass killings of dodos for ships' provisions, archaeological investigations have found scant evidence of human predation.

facts.statement: The impact of introduced animals, particularly pigs and macaques, on the dodo population is considered more severe than the impact of hunting.
facts.quote: The impact of the introduced animals on the dodo population, especially the pigs and macaques, is today considered more severe than that of hunting.

facts.statement: Rats were perhaps not a major threat to dodo nests because dodos were likely accustomed to dealing with local land crabs.
facts.quote: Rats were perhaps not much of a threat to the nests, since dodos would have been used to dealing with local land crabs.

facts.statement: A 2005 expedition discovered subfossil remains of dodos and other animals that had been killed by a flash flood.
facts.quote: A 2005 expedition found subfossil remains of dodos and other animals killed by a flash flood.

facts.statement: A 2003 statistical analysis by biologists David L. Roberts and Andrew R. Solow estimated the dodo's extinction date to be 1693, with a 95% confidence interval of 1688–1715.
facts.quote: A 2003 statistical analysis of these records by the biologists David L. Roberts and Andrew R. Solow gave a new estimated extinction date of 1693, with a 95% confidence interval of 1688–1715.

facts.statement: There is controversy surrounding the exact date of the dodo's extinction.
facts.quote: Some controversy surrounds the date of the dodo's extinction.

facts.statement: It is debated whether descriptions of "Dodo" and "Dodaers" after 1662 actually refer to the dodo or have been transferred to the red rail.
facts.quote: Cheke also pointed out that some descriptions after 1662 use the names "Dodo" and "Dodaers" when referring to the red rail, indicating that they had been transferred to it.

facts.statement: In 2014, Cheke stated that Dutch manuscripts indicate no dodos were seen by settlers between 1664 and 1674.
facts.quote: Cheke stated in 2014 that then recently accessible Dutch manuscripts indicate that no dodos were seen by settlers in 1664–1674.

facts.statement: It is unlikely the debate over the dodo's extinction date will be resolved unless late reports with physical descriptions are rediscovered.
facts.quote: It is unlikely the issue will ever be resolved, unless late reports mentioning the name alongside a physical description are rediscovered.

facts.statement: The IUCN Red List accepts the rationale for choosing 1662 as the extinction date, treating all subsequent reports as referring to red rails.
facts.quote: The IUCN Red List accepts Cheke's rationale for choosing the 1662 date, taking all subsequent reports to refer to red rails.

facts.statement: The dodo was probably extinct by 1700, approximately a century after its discovery in 1598.
facts.quote: In any case, the dodo was probably extinct by 1700, about a century after its discovery in 1598.

facts.statement: The only surviving physical remains of dodos brought to Europe in the 17th century include a dried head and foot in Oxford, a skull in Copenhagen, and an upper jaw in Prague.
facts.quote: The only extant remains of dodo specimens taken to Europe in the 17th century are a dried head and foot in the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, a foot once housed in the British Museum but now lost, a skull in the University of Copenhagen Zoological Museum, and an upper jaw in the National Museum, Prague.

facts.statement: The Copenhagen skull and the Prague upper jaw were not identified as dodo remains until the mid-19th century.
facts.quote: The last two were rediscovered and identified as dodo remains in the mid-19th century.

facts.statement: A dried dodo foot belonging to Pieter Pauw was recorded by Carolus Clusius in 1605, though it is now lost.
facts.quote: A dried foot which belonged to Dutch professor Pieter Pauw was mentioned by Carolus Clusius in 1605.

facts.statement: Many stuffed dodos currently displayed in museums are fakes made from the feathers of other birds, often produced by Rowland Ward's company.
facts.quote: Purported stuffed dodos seen in museums around the world today have in fact been made from feathers of other birds; many by British taxidermist Rowland Ward's company.

facts.statement: The only known soft tissue remains of a dodo, a head and a foot, were part of the Tradescant collection mentioned in 1656 and moved to the Ashmolean Museum in 1659.
facts.quote: The only known soft tissue remains, the Oxford head (specimen OUM 11605) and foot, belonged to the last known stuffed dodo, which was first mentioned as part of the Tradescant collection in 1656 and was moved to the Ashmolean Museum in 1659.

facts.statement: Scans of the Oxford dodo head reported in 2018 revealed lead shot embedded in the skin and bone, indicating it was hunted in the 17th century.
facts.quote: In 2018, it was reported that scans of the Oxford dodo's head showed that its skin and bone contained lead shot, which was used to hunt birds in the 17th century.

facts.statement: The Oxford dodo specimen was displayed at the museum from the 1860s until 1998 before being moved to storage.
facts.quote: The specimen was exhibited at the Oxford museum from at least the 1860s and until 1998, where-after it was mainly kept in storage to prevent damage.

facts.statement: The lack of a standing posture in the London foot suggests it was cut from a fresh specimen rather than a taxidermy mount.
facts.quote: It was not posed in a standing posture, which suggests that it was severed from a fresh specimen, not a mounted one.

facts.statement: By 1896 the London foot was known to lack skin, and only its bones are believed to remain, though their current location is unknown.
facts.quote: By 1896 it was mentioned as being without its integuments, and only the bones are believed to remain today, though its present whereabouts are unknown.

facts.statement: The Copenhagen skull was part of Bernardus Paludanus's collection in Enkhuizen until 1651, when it was transferred to the museum at Gottorf Castle.
facts.quote: The Copenhagen skull (specimen ZMUC 90-806) is known to have been part of the collection of Bernardus Paludanus in Enkhuizen until 1651, when it was moved to the museum in Gottorf Castle, Schleswig.

facts.statement: The Copenhagen skull was rediscovered by J. T. Reinhardt in 1840.
facts.quote: The skull was rediscovered by J. T. Reinhardt in 1840.

facts.statement: Based on its history, the Copenhagen skull may be the oldest known surviving dodo remains brought to Europe in the 17th century.
facts.quote: Based on its history, it may be the oldest known surviving remains of a dodo brought to Europe in the 17th century.

facts.statement: A partial dodo skull was found in the National Museum of Prague in 1850 among the remains of the Böhmisches Museum.
facts.quote: The front part of a skull (specimen NMP P6V-004389) in the National Museum of Prague was found in 1850 among the remains of the Böhmisches Museum.

facts.statement: The Prague skull fragment may be the remains of a stuffed dodo from Emperor Rudolph II's menagerie, possibly the one painted by Jacob Hoefnagel or Savery.
facts.quote: It may be what remains of one of the stuffed dodos known to have been at the menagerie of Emperor Rudolph II, possibly the specimen painted by Jacob Hoefnagel or Savery there.

facts.statement: The first subfossil dodo bones were discovered in 1860 by Philip Burnard Ayres.
facts.quote: Philip Burnard Ayres found the first subfossil bones in 1860

facts.statement: George Clark discovered a large number of dodo bones in the Mare aux Songes swamp in Southern Mauritius in 1865.
facts.quote: In 1865, George Clark, the government schoolmaster at Mahébourg, finally found an abundance of subfossil dodo bones in the swamp of Mare aux Songes in Southern Mauritius

facts.statement: The Mare aux Songes swamp yielded the remains of more than 300 dodos.
facts.quote: The swamp yielded the remains of over 300 dodos

facts.statement: A complete dodo skeleton was discovered in a lava cave in Mauritius in 2006.
facts.quote: In 2006, explorers discovered a complete skeleton of a dodo in a lava cave in Mauritius

facts.statement: An international team excavated a section of the Mare aux Songes swamp in 2005.
facts.quote: In 2005, after a hundred years of neglect, a part of the Mare aux Songes swamp was excavated by an international team of researchers

facts.statement: The dodo is classified in the kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Aves, order Columbiformes, family Columbidae, subfamily Raphinae, and genus Raphus.
facts.quote: regnum: Animalia phylum: Chordata classis: Aves ordo: Columbiformes familia: Columbidae subfamilia: Raphinae genus: Raphus

facts.statement: The scientific name of the dodo is Raphus cucullatus, originally described by Linnaeus in 1758.
facts.quote: species: R. cucullatus species_authority: (Linnaeus, 1758)

facts.statement: The dodo became extinct in 1690.
facts.quote: extinct: 1690

facts.statement: The dodo was native to the island of Mauritius.
facts.quote: range_map: Mauritius island location.svg

facts.statement: The existence of a distinct white dodo species on Réunion is now considered an erroneous conjecture.
facts.quote: The supposed "white dodo" (or "solitaire") of Réunion is now considered an erroneous conjecture

facts.statement: It is debated whether the white coloration in dodo paintings represented albinism, juvenile plumage, bleaching of old specimens, or artistic license.
facts.quote: Valledor de Lozoya has instead suggested that the light plumage was a juvenile trait, a result of bleaching of old taxidermy specimens, or simply artistic license

facts.statement: Fossils from the Mare aux Songes swamp show that dodos likely died trapped in the mud with their lower bodies preserved while their upper bodies were washed away or scavenged.
facts.quote: The swamp yielded the remains of over 300 dodos, but very few skull and wing bones, possibly because the upper bodies were washed away or scavenged while the lower body was trapped

facts.statement: Most dodo bones recovered from the Mare aux Songes swamp have a medium to dark brown coloration.
facts.quote: Most dodo remains from the Mare aux Songes have a medium to dark brown colouration

facts.statement: In 2011, a box of dodo bones from the Edwardian era was rediscovered at the Grant Museum, University College London, where they had been stored with crocodile bones.
facts.quote: In 2011, a wooden box containing dodo bones from the Edwardian era was rediscovered at the Grant Museum at University College London during preparations for a move. They had been stored with crocodile bones until then

facts.statement: There are significant dodo collections in 26 museums worldwide, almost all derived from the Mare aux Songes swamp.
facts.quote: Worldwide, 26 museums have significant holdings of dodo material, almost all found in the Mare aux Songes

facts.statement: The dodo was a flightless bird endemic to Mauritius, located in the Indian Ocean 900 km from Madagascar.
facts.quote: Era un ave no voladora endémica de la isla Mauricio, situada en el océano Índico (a 900 km de la isla de Madagascar).

facts.statement: The closest living relative of the dodo is likely the Nicobar pigeon, an endemic species of certain islands in the Indian Ocean.
facts.quote: El pariente vivo más próximo al dodo es probablemente la paloma de Nicobar, una especie de paloma endémica de ciertas islas del océano Índico.

facts.statement: Other publications estimate the dodo's weight ranged between 9.5 and 17.5 kg.
facts.quote: Sin embargo otras publicaciones estiman un rango de entre 9,5 y 17,5 kg.

facts.statement: The dodo had a very long beak, approximately 23 cm, with a hook-shaped tip that likely allowed it to break coconut shells.
facts.quote: Su pico era muy largo, aproximadamente de 23 cm, y con una punta en forma de garfio que probablemente le permitía romper las cortezas de los cocos.

facts.statement: The dodo had yellow, robust legs with a few curled feathers on the back part.
facts.quote: Sus patas eran amarillas y robustas, con unas cuantas plumas rizadas en su parte de atrás.

facts.statement: Today, the general scientific opinion is that old drawings of the dodo depicted captive individuals that had been overfed.
facts.quote: Hoy en día, la opinión general de la comunidad científica es que los viejos dibujos del dodo retrataban a ejemplares cautivos que habían sido sobrealimentados.

facts.statement: The first news of the bird in Europe seem to date from 1574, and in 1581 the Spanish conquistador Agustín Agüero brought a specimen to Europe.
facts.quote: Las primeras noticias que se tuvieron en Europa del ave parecen datar de 1574; en 1581 el conquistador español Agustín Agüero, llevó un ejemplar a Europa.

facts.statement: The last specimen was seen for the last time in 1662, though there is a sighting by a runaway slave in 1674, and it is believed to have existed until 1690.
facts.quote: El último ejemplar fue visto por última vez en 1662, aunque existe un avistamiento por parte de un esclavo cimarrón en 1674, y se cree que debió de existir hasta 1690.

facts.statement: It is calculated that the raiding of nests by new species had a more devastating effect than hunting; specifically, pigs brought by humans to the island destroyed the dodo's eggs by raiding and eating them.
facts.quote: Se calcula que el saqueo de sus nidos por parte de las nuevas especies tuvo un efecto más devastador que el de la caza. En particular, los cerdos llevados por el ser humano a la isla acabaron con los huevos de esta ave, pues asaltaban sus nidos y se los comían.

facts.statement: In June 2007, adventurers exploring a cave in Mauritius found, to date, the most complete and best-preserved dodo skeleton.
facts.quote: En junio de 2007, unos aventureros explorando una cueva en las Islas Mauricio encontraron, hasta el momento, el más completo y mejor conservado esqueleto de dodo.

facts.statement: One of the most intact remains, and the only ones preserving some soft tissue, are those exhibited at the University of Oxford's Natural History Museum, consisting of the head and legs of a single individual.
facts.quote: Uno de los restos que se han conservado más intactos y los únicos que han conservado algo de tejido blando son los que se exponen en el Museo de Historia Natural de la Universidad de Oxford; consistentes en la cabeza y las patas de un mismo individuo.

facts.statement: His theory had certain points left unclear, such as the fact that it was not verified how the germination of other fruits worked after being eaten by turkeys, so the demonstrated effect was not entirely clear.
facts.quote: Su teoría tenía ciertos puntos sin esclarecer, como el que no se comprobó cómo funcionaba la germinación de otras frutas tras ser comidas por pavos, con lo que el efecto demostrado no quedó del todo claro.

facts.statement: Furthermore, Temple did not take into account reports on the germination of tambalacoque seeds from A. W. Hill in 1941 and H. C. King in 1946, who discovered that the seeds germinated without prior corrosion, although very rarely.
facts.quote: Además Temple no tuvo en cuenta los informes sobre la germinación de las semillas de tambalacoque de la germinación de otras frutas de A. W. Hill en 1941 y de H. C. King en 1946, quienes descubrieron que las semillas germinaban sin necesidad de corrosión previa, aunque muy raramente.

facts.statement: The coat of arms of Mauritius features a dodo in a rampant position.
facts.quote: El escudo de Mauricio incorpora un dodo rampante.

facts.statement: The asteroid (6336) Dodo was named in reference to this bird.
facts.quote: El asteroide (6336) Dodo fue nombrado así en referencia a esta ave.

facts.statement: Geneticists and conservationists plan to resurrect the extinct dodo and reintroduce it to Mauritius.
facts.quote: Genetistas y conservacionistas planean resucitar al extinto dodo y reintroducirlo en Mauricio.

facts.statement: The company Colossal Biosciences has partnered with the Mauritian Wildlife Foundation for this de-extinction project.
facts.quote: La empresa Colossal Biosciences se asocia con la Mauritian Wildlife Foundation para este proyecto de desextinción.

facts.statement: Scientists have sequenced the dodo's genome along with those of close relatives, such as the Nicobar pigeon.
facts.quote: Han secuenciado el genoma del dodo y de parientes cercanos, como la paloma de Nicobar.

facts.statement: Colossal Biosciences plans to edit the germline cells of the pigeon to express dodo traits and create hybrid birds through reproduction.
facts.quote: Colossal planea editar células germinales de la paloma para que expresen rasgos de dodo y, mediante la reproducción, crear aves híbridas.

facts.statement: The Mauritian Wildlife Foundation is searching for suitable locations in Mauritius for the reintroduction of the dodo.
facts.quote: La Mauritian Wildlife Foundation busca ubicaciones adecuadas en Mauricio para la reintroducción.

facts.statement: While the project generates enthusiasm, some experts warn about its complexity and question its priority compared to conventional conservation efforts.
facts.quote: Aunque el proyecto genera entusiasmo, algunos expertos advierten sobre la complejidad y cuestionan su prioridad frente a la conservación convencional.

facts.statement: The genus Raphus was named by Brisson in 1760.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Raphus (genus), Brisson 1760
